newsitem.title: USA: US Army names 2 to suspended sergeant major's job.
newsitem.headline: US Army names 2 to suspended sergeant major's job.

text.p: The U.S. Army named two acting sergeants major on Friday to fill in for Sgt. Maj. Gene McKinney, who was suspended as the top enlisted man amid allegations of sexual harassment.
The two acting sergeants major, one of whom is McKinney's twin brother, will take turns doing the job until the case against McKinney is resolved, the Army said in a statement.
At the same time, the Army announced that its sexual harassment hotline would cease operating on Friday, saying it "has done its job."

"It is in the best interest of the Army and our soldiers will be better served by having an experienced command sergeant major performing duties traditionally performed by the sergeant major of the Army," Army Chief of Staff Gen. Dennis Reimer said. "It is essential we have someone performing these critical duties during this important period in our nation's history."

McKinney was suspended in February from his Pentagon job as the senior enlisted adviser to service leaders pending resolution of sexual harassment allegations against him by former soldier Brenda Hoster. In May, the Army charged the 22-year veteran with adultery and indecent assault against four servicewomen, adding to the scandal over sexual harassment in the U.S. military.

The three other women who alleged that McKinney acted inappropriately with them have been questioned extensively by Army investigators. Charges against McKinney include four counts of maltreatment of soldiers, two counts of assault, one of adultery, two of communicating a threat and three of soliciting adultery.
McKinney has denied the charges and has asked for permission to retire to avoid the possibility of a court-martial.
The new appointees are Command Sgt. Maj. Jerry Alley, currently assigned to U.S. Forces Command, and Command Sgt. Maj. James McKinney, currently assigned to the Army's Training and Doctrine Command.

Meanwhile, the Army's sexual harassment hotline, which was set up last November, was to end operations on Friday and will be supplanted in 30 days or less by a sexual harassment and sexual abuse assistance line. The Army said the hotline had served its purpose and the high volume of calls received when it was first established had dwindled in recent weeks.

The new assistance line will offer counselling and provide information to victims about assistance, reporting procedures and channels. It will augment the Army's other avenues for reporting grievances, which include the service's inspector general, military police and criminal investigation units, chaplains, chains of command and equal opportunity counsellors.
